churn_timeline.event: Onboarded on a referral from client Chey Mai. Five topics created; Mica, Michelle and Mayson introduce themselves with self-serve links.

FIRST WARNING SIGN, and it is ours, not hers. Twelve days in she has seen neither the invoice nor the content request: 'oh i didnt see this sorry im new to telegram'. Nobody had checked. She says she will book Mica's call - she never does and Mica never chases it in the remaining 67 days.

Vivek is introduced as Meta Support Rep. Within minutes she reports she cannot share links and, at his request, posts her Instagram login and password in plaintext in the group. He fixes it the same hour.
Derrek's phone-farm broadcast. She replies with the warmest message of the relationship. The promised 'plenty of updates starting next week' never arrive - 41 days.
Instagram lockout episode 2. Vivek says 'Send login in dm'; she posts the credentials in the group again. He goes quiet for two hours.

Vivek asks her to approve a login for an account that is not hers - 'Unfilteredlifiting'. She replies 'what the hell hold on'. His last word on it that day is 'Hell nah'. She is never told whether her account was cross-linked to another client's. He also promises 'Will update shortly' and never does.
Invoice issued announcing a CHANGED ACCOUNT NUMBER and new Zelle details inside the payment request.
Lockout episode 3. Two more plaintext credential posts. Fixed in seven minutes - the single best moment on the account, and she thanks us twice.

Lockout episode 4 opens. Vivek asks for a screenshot and then does not return to it. Sixteen days later she leaves with it still unresolved. The same day Stephski nudges her for payment; she had already paid - 'i already sent it babe x'.

Three more credential and approval demands from Vivek, producing a sixth plaintext password post. Mayson issues a 30-reels-a-month content quota into the same Drive folder Michelle had already requested uploads to in July. Vivek's final message on the account is another request from her: 'Need approval for the account'.

THE PROXIMATE TRIGGER. She reports a serious new problem: 'ive got a leak. someone using my stuff on a swingers website x'. Michelle answers within 7 hours after 44 days of silence and claims it. The same evening Mica reappears after 18 days - not with help, but with a lecture about consistent posting, to a client whose Instagram was still broken.
She supplies the exact leak URL. Nobody has ever replied to it. Nick (DMCA), the named owner of that function with a dedicated topic in this chat since day one, was never brought in.
Sep 1 invoice issued with 'I ask that you please pay within 7 days to avoid any pausing of work'. Four asks in five days and zero deliverables.

RESIGNATION: 'hey!! i just wanted to inform that i'm leaving the agency tomorrow! thank you for what you have been doing but its just not working for me I'm sorry!'. Her leak request had been in a void for roughly 31 hours.
Mayson offers a call 72 minutes later - the only reply anyone ever made to the resignation. She does not answer and nobody re-offers.
Seven days of silence, then two collections chases. The first threatens 'we will have to pause work in the morning'. That threat is the last thing Paige has heard from ALTR.
An unidentified account is added to the chat and posts nothing.

Twenty-three days after the resignation: no owner contact, no exit conversation, no ledger reconciliation, the leak still unanswered at 25 days, the fourth lockout never closed, and six plaintext credential messages of hers still sitting in the group.

warning_signs_missed: Every client-initiated thread in 79 days was an account-access emergency and not one of them was ever closed with an explanation - the clearest possible signal that she was getting no service, only incidents.

Four forced Instagram resets in 30 days is not client error. Nobody ever tested whether our own phone-farm login pattern was tripping Meta's checks, which would make this a systemic defect live on every account on that system.
She spent a month guessing at what was happening to her own accounts ('thinking i was hacled') and lost track of her own password. Confusion at that level is a churn precursor.
We asked her to approve a login for a different client's account and never explained it. She was left believing her account might have been cross-linked to someone else's.

Asks and bills vastly outnumbered deliverables in her final fortnight: three credential demands, a 30-reels monthly quota, a posting-consistency lecture, an invoice with a pause threat, and zero output.

Mica's first message in 18 days was a lecture about posting consistency sent to a creator whose Instagram had locked four times in 30 days - the tone-deafness of that message should have been caught before it went out.
Her leak report on 2026-08-31 was the highest-urgency thing she ever raised; it was claimed and then dropped, and she resigned roughly 31 hours after supplying the URL.

A client who apologises in nearly every message and never complains is not a healthy client - she absorbed four lockouts, seven credential requests and a content quota without pushback, which removed every visible early warning.
Her resignation was answered once, by the wrong seniority, and never escalated to the owner - and then collections ran on her anyway seven days later.
She is Chey Mai's referral, and Chey Mai was herself being chased for unpaid invoices at the same time. Nobody joined those two dots or got ahead of what the referrer would hear.
